The King and I. The nineteen fifty-one musical by Richard Rodgers, music, and Oscar Hammerstein II, lyrics, based on Margaret Landon's novel Anna and the King of Siam. Set in nineteenth-century Bangkok, it follows the cultural and romantic tension between Anna Leonowens, a headstrong British widow hired as a tutor to the royal children, and King Mongkut of Siam, an autocrat attempting to modernize his kingdom while preserving its traditions.

This was their third major collaboration, running for twelve hundred forty-six performances on Broadway from nineteen fifty-one to nineteen fifty-four. The opening number "I Whistle a Happy Tune" establishes Anna's courage and self-reliance. Other major songs include "Shall We Dance," "Getting to Know You," "Something Wonderful," and "We Kiss in a Shadow." The "Shall We Dance" sequence, in which Anna and the King dance together in formal Western dress, becomes a symbol of mutual respect and cultural bridging across their differences.

Based on Margaret Landon's semi-fictionalized biography of the real Anna Leonowens, who served as tutor to the Thai royal family in the eighteen sixty.

The show won five Tony Awards in nineteen fifty-two. The nineteen fifty-six film, directed by Walter Lang and starring Deborah Kerr and Yul Brynner, won five Academy Awards and became a cultural touchstone. Yul Brynner originated the role of the King and became synonymous with it, famously reprising the role in the nineteen eighty-five Broadway revival, his final performance.

The musical deftly balances the romance between Anna and the King with the larger theme of East-West cross-cultural understanding, prefiguring later explorations of cultural friction and mutual recognition.
